title: Building a RAG Pipeline from Scratch with Python and Pinecone
excerpt: A practical guide to building retrieval-augmented generation systems â€” from document chunking and embeddings to semantic search and LLM grounding.
content:
## What is RAG?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that combines the power of large language models with external knowledge retrieval. Instead of relying solely on the model's training data, RAG systems fetch relevant documents at query time and use them to ground the LLM's responses.

## Why RAG Matters

Traditional LLMs have a cutoff date and can hallucinate facts. RAG solves this by:

- **Grounding responses in real data** â€” the model cites actual documents
- **Reducing hallucinations** â€” answers are backed by retrieved context
- **Keeping knowledge fresh** â€” no retraining needed for new documents
- **Providing source attribution** â€” users can verify where answers come from

## Architecture Overview

A typical RAG pipeline consists of three stages:

### 1. Document Ingestion

We load documents, split them into chunks, and generate embeddings for each chunk.

### 2. Vector Storage

Each chunk gets embedded using a model like OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small and stored in a vector database like Pinecone.

### 3. Query & Generation

At query time, we embed the user's question, find the most similar chunks, and pass them as context to the LLM.

## Key Design Decisions

Chunk quality matters more than quantity. Better chunking beats more chunks.

Metadata filtering is powerful. Adding category/date filters before vector search improved relevance by 23%.

## Conclusion

RAG is not just a trend â€” it's the practical path to building AI systems that are grounded, verifiable, and useful.

title: Why Campus Fintech is the Next Big Thing in Africa
excerpt: The untapped potential of campus payment systems, student wallets, and micro-financial services across African universities.
content:
## The Campus Payment Gap

African universities process billions in transactions annually â€” tuition, meals, supplies, services â€” yet most of this happens in cash or through clunky, outdated systems.

## The Opportunity

Students are digital natives who need:
- Wallet-based payments for campus services
- Micro-loans and credit facilities
- Savings tools for financial discipline
- Merchant integration for campus businesses

## Why Now

Smartphone penetration, mobile money adoption, and regulatory openness create the perfect conditions for campus fintech.

## Conclusion

The campus is Africa's most concentrated market. Win there, and you build the financial habits of an entire generation.

title: Lessons from Building kwestpay: A Developer's Retrospective
excerpt: What I learned building a campus fintech platform from zero â€” technical decisions, architecture trade-offs, and user adoption challenges.
content:
## Starting from Zero

When I started kwestpay, I had a clear vision: make campus payments seamless. The reality was far more complex.

## Technical Decisions

### The Stack

React + Node.js + MongoDB. Not the flashiest, but the fastest to ship.

### Payment Integration

Flutterwave for card payments, bank transfer for larger amounts. The key was making both feel identical to the user.

## What Worked

- Building the MVP in 3 weeks
- Onboarding 50 users in the first week
- Getting campus vendor buy-in early

## What Didn't

- Over-engineering the wallet system
- Not investing in fraud detection early enough
- Ignoring offline scenarios

## Lessons

Ship fast, learn fast. The best architecture is the one that gets you to the next user.

title: Food Credits and the Future of FoodTech in Nigeria
excerpt: How credit-based food systems can bridge the gap between food vendors and consumers in emerging markets.
content:
## The Food Problem

Nigeria wastes 40% of its food production due to poor logistics, lack of credit, and disconnected supply chains.

## Food Credits as a Solution

A credit-based system lets consumers access food now and pay later, while vendors get guaranteed revenue and reduced waste.

## How It Works

1. Consumers get a credit limit based on verified identity
2. Vendors accept credits with guaranteed settlement
3. The platform handles reconciliation and fraud prevention

## The Impact

Reduced food waste, increased vendor revenue, and better food access for consumers.

## Conclusion

FoodTech in Nigeria isn't about delivery apps â€” it's about rebuilding the food value chain from the ground up.

title: I'm not a fan of ceremonies but this was indispensable.
excerpt: After 6 years of highs and lows, I got inducted into the society of Engineers; What happened before and in the hall was breathtakingly glorious for me.
content:
## The ceremony

Today I got inducted.

Cap, gown, ceremony, photographs, the whole ritual. And somewhere between the opening prayer and the closing anthem, a question kept running through my head:

What was I doing with the other hours? 



## The other thing I was building

Alongside the lectures and the lab reports, I was shipping products into the real world. Hardware and Software that people found, used, paid for, and complained about. I only wanted to solve problems in the world with whatever I've got in my hands. 

The numbers are not Silicon Valley numbers. They are honest ones:

- $16.6K in revenue, year one, bootstrapped
- 5,000+ users across all products
- 6,422+ transactions processed

Four products went live out of 7: a FinTech payment product, an EdTech platform,  an AI tool and an harware that got recognized by the government (thank you, TRV :) ). In July 2025, the African Stable-coin Network recognized me for leadership on Africa's digital economy. That recognition did not come from a transcript. It came from a mind open for observation and  shipping to fill the gaps.

## What the building taught me that the lectures did not

School gave me the theory. Production gave me the consequences. School gave me the grit, production gave the assurances.

### Users do not care about the technological stack

Nobody has ever left a product because you chose FastAPI over Express. They leave because it was slow, confusing, or broken when they needed it.They leave because it didn't solve their issues but added to it. 
Pick tools for speed of shipping, not for your resume.

### Revenue is feedback that cannot lie

People will praise a demo to be polite. They will not pay to be polite. The first payment turned a project into a business, and it ended every argument I was having with myself about what to build next.

### Distribution is harder than engineering

You can write clean, tested, beautifully architected code and still have zero users. I now spend more time on "how does someone find this?" than on "how do I build this?" That ratio is correct. It just took me a while to accept it.

### Ship the ugly version this week

Perfect code or firmware that nobody uses is a private journal entry. Ugly code that 500 people use is a product with a feedback loop. Refactor after you know what matters. I was keen on shipping even though it wasn't perfect at the beginning.

### The expensive bug is usually in the assumption

Syntax bugs are cheap. The costly ones are building the wrong thing confidently for three weeks. Now I write the assumption down before I write the code: who wants this, how often, and what do they do today instead?

### Consistency beats intensity

Nobody remembers the all-nighter. They remember the product still standing twelve months later. The work that compounds is the boring kind: small releases, replies to users, fixing the thing everyone complained about, repeating it next week.

## What the degree means now

The degree is not a receipt for what I already built. It is permission to build bigger, with less excuse.

If you are still in school and reading this: the fastest way to be taken seriously after graduation is to already have something in the world that people use. Start embarrassingly small. Ship this week.


What is the one thing school did not teach you? I am collecting answers.
